extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate or beginning graduate students in algebraic topology / mathematicians learning homology theory
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of singular and cellular homology: Mayer–Vietoris sequences, homology with coefficients, mapping torus exact sequence, axioms for (reduced) homology theories, and functorial formulation. Intended as instructional material for computing and understanding homology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayer–Vietoris short exact sequence of chain complexes
rubrics_metrics.description: For X = A ∪ B define Cn(A + B) as subgroup of Cn(X) of sums of chains in A and chains in B. There is a short exact sequence of chain complexes 0 → Cn(A ∩ B) --ϕ→ Cn(A) ⊕ Cn(B) --ψ→ Cn(A + B) → 0 with ϕ(x) = (x, −x) and ψ(x, y) = x + y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exactness is checked by: Ker ϕ = 0, Im ϕ ⊂ Ker ψ since ψϕ = 0, Ker ψ ⊂ Im ϕ because x + y = 0 ⇒ x = −y so x ∈ Cn(A ∩ B), and exactness at Cn(A + B) is immediate from the definition of Cn(A + B). These short exact sequences of chain complexes are the input to derive the Mayer–Vietoris long exact sequence on homology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayer–Vietoris long exact sequence on homology
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mayer–Vietoris sequence is the long exact sequence of homology groups associated to the short exact sequence of chain complexes arising from 0 → Cn(A ∩ B) → Cn(A)⊕Cn(B) → Cn(A+B) → 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The boundary map ∂ : Hn(X) → Hn−1(A ∩ B) is made explicit: represent α ∈ Hn(X) by a cycle z, choose a subdivision so z = x + y with x in A and y in B; while x and y may not be cycles individually, ∂x = −∂y and ∂α is represented by ∂x = −∂y. There is an analogous reduced Mayer–Vietoris sequence obtained by augmenting the short exact sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced Mayer–Vietoris sequence and relation to van Kampen/abelianization
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a formally identical Mayer–Vietoris sequence for reduced homology groups, obtained by augmenting the previous short exact sequence of chain complexes in the obvious way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If A ∩ B is path-connected, the H1 terms of the reduced Mayer–Vietoris sequence yield an isomorphism H1(X) ≈ (H1(A) ⊕ H1(B)) / Im Φ, which is exactly the abelianized form of van Kampen since H1 is the abelianization of π1 for path-connected spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayer–Vietoris under deformation-retract neighborhood hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: If A and B are deformation retracts of neighborhoods U and V with U ∩ V deformation retracting onto A ∩ B (e.g., X a CW complex and A,B subcomplexes with suitable neighborhoods), then the maps Cn(A + B) → Cn(U + V) induce isomorphisms on homology and hence yield a Mayer–Vietoris sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The five-lemma is used: Cn(A + B) → Cn(U + V) inducing isomorphisms on homology implies Cn(A + B) → Cn(X) induce isomorphisms, so the same short exact sequence construction applies. Example: choose neighborhoods Nε(A), Nε(B) with Nε(A) ∩ Nε(B) = Nε(A ∩ B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping torus / quotient exact sequence (f∗ − g∗)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given maps f,g : X → Y form quotient space Z by attaching ends of X × I to Y via f and g. There is a long exact sequence ··· → Hn(X) --f∗−g∗→ Hn(Y) --i∗→ Hn(Z) → Hn−1(X) --f∗−g∗→ Hn−1(Y) → ··· where i is inclusion Y ↪ Z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation: consider q : (X × I, X × ∂I) → (Z, Y) induced by the quotient map and map long exact sequences; kernel of i∗ consists of pairs (α, −α) in Hn(X) ⊕ Hn(X) and the middle vertical map q∗ takes (α, −α) to f∗(α) − g∗(α). Special cases: mapping torus, double mapping cylinder, Klein bottle examples arising from choices of f,g.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative Mayer–Vietoris sequence for pairs
rubrics_metrics.description: If (X, Y) = (A ∪ B, C ∪ D) with C ⊂ A, D ⊂ B and X,Y unions of interiors as required, there is a relative Mayer–Vietoris long exact sequence ··· → Hn(A ∩ B, C ∩ D) → Hn(A, C) ⊕ Hn(B, D) → Hn(X, Y) → Hn−1(A ∩ B, C ∩ D) → ···
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction uses a commutative diagram of chain complexes where Cn(A + B, C + D) = Cn(A + B)/Cn(C + D). Exactness of rows and columns (plus the five-lemma/functorial arguments) yields the long exact sequence associated to the third row short exact sequence of chain complexes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homology with coefficients in an abelian group G (definition and basics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace integer coefficients by an abelian group G: chains are formal sums ∑ niσi with ni ∈ G, forming groups Cn(X; G); boundary formula ∂ still applies and ∂^2 = 0. Relative groups Cn(X, A; G) = Cn(X; G)/Cn(A; G). Reduced groups Hn(X; G) defined via the augmented chain complex ··· → C0(X; G) →ε G → 0 with ε summing coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All earlier theory for Z coefficients carries over directly with identical proofs. The special case G = Z2 is simpler: coefficients 0 or 1 allow thinking of chains as finite unions of simplices; signs/orientations vanish, so Z2-homology is convenient when orientability is an issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cellular homology with coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: Cellular chain group Hn(Xn, Xn−1; G) is a direct sum of copies of G, one for each n-cell. The cellular homology H^CW_n(X; G) agrees with singular homology Hn(X; G). The cellular boundary maps are given by the same formulas as for Z coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The old proof that cellular homology equals singular homology extends immediately. One only needs to know that the cellular coefficients d_{αβ} are the same as before (i.e., independent of chosen coefficient group), so boundary formulas carry over.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 2.49: degree action on homology with coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : S^k → S^k has degree m, then f∗ : Hk(S^k; G) → Hk(S^k; G) is multiplication by m.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: use a homomorphism ϕ : Z → G taking 1 ↦ g ∈ G to form a commutative diagram relating Hk with Z-coefficients and G-coefficients; the top map sends 1 ↦ m, so the bottom sends g ↦ mg. Naturalities of induced maps and the inductive calculation of homology groups are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic calculated values with coefficients (point and spheres)
rubrics_metrics.description: When X is a point, Hn(X; G) is G for n = 0 and 0 for n > 0. Consequently Hn(S^k; G) is G for n = k and 0 otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These follow by the same methods as for integer coefficients and are used as base cases in many inductive homology computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior of RP^n homology with field coefficients (illustrative example)
rubrics_metrics.description: For RP^n and coefficients in a field F the cellular chain complex alternates maps that are multiplication by 2 between copies of F. If char(F) = 2 (e.g., F = Z2) then Hk(RP^n; F) ≈ F for 0 ≤ k ≤ n. If char(F) ≠ 2 then the maps ‘2: F → F’ are isomorphisms, yielding Hk(RP^n; F) ≈ F for k = 0 and for k = n odd, and zero otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This example highlights how choice of coefficient field changes homology calculations—torsion in integral homology can disappear or become uniform depending on characteristic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short exact sequence relating homology with Z_n coefficients and torsion (exercise statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are short exact sequences 0 → Hi(X)/nHi(X) → Hi(X; Z_n) → n-Torsion(Hi−1(X)) → 0, where n-Torsion(G) is the kernel of multiplication-by-n map G → G, g ↦ ng.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the short exact sequence of chain complexes 0 → Ci(X) → Ci(X; Z_n) → 0 and algebraic consequences to deduce this; corollaries include characterizations of when Hi(X; Z_p) vanish and relations to Hi(X) being a Q-vector space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms for a (reduced) homology theory (Eilenberg–Steenrod style)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reduced homology theory assigns groups h_n(X) to CW complexes and homomorphisms f∗ to maps f : X → Y such that (f g)∗ = f∗ g∗ and 1∗ = 1, and satisfies: (1) homotopy invariance: f ≃ g ⇒ f∗ = g∗; (2) long exact sequence axiom: for each CW pair (X,A) there are boundary homomorphisms ∂ fitting into a natural long exact sequence ··· → h_n(A) → h_n(X) → h_n(X/A) → h_{n−1}(A) → ···; (3) wedge axiom: for wedge sums X = ∨ X_α the direct sum map ⊕ h_n(X_α) → h_n(X) is an isomorphism for each n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Axioms specialize appropriately for unreduced theories (replace wedge by disjoint union; include excision). The dimension axiom (h_n(point)=0 for n ≠ 0) can be added as a normalization (as in Eilenberg–Steenrod); failure of this axiom yields theories like bordism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of reduced and unreduced homology and coefficient groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduced and unreduced homology theories are essentially equivalent: from an unreduced theory h define reduced hn(X) = ker(hn(X) → hn(point)). Conversely set hn(X) = h_n(X+) where X+ is X with a disjoint basepoint. Coefficient groups are hn(point) ≈ hn(S^0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These transformations are inverses; for any desired sequence of coefficient groups G_i one can realize them by setting hn(X,A) = ⊕_i H_{n−i}(X,A; G_i). For singular homology, if coeﬃcient groups vanish except in degree 0 then the theory is naturally isomorphic to H*(−; G).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayer–Vietoris derivable from homology axioms for CW complexes
rubrics_metrics.description: For a CW complex X = A ∪ B with A,B subcomplexes, inclusion (B, A∩B) ↪ (X, A) induces a commutative diagram of exact sequences. Two of the three vertical maps are isomorphisms, and an algebraic lemma (exercise 38) gives rise to the Mayer–Vietoris long exact sequence ··· → h_n(A∩B) → h_n(A) ⊕ h_n(B) → h_n(X) → h_{n−1}(A∩B) → ···.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shows MV is a formal consequence of the axioms; in general any homology theory for CW complexes satisfying the axioms has Mayer–Vietoris sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functoriality requirements and functor examples (homology as a functor)
rubrics_metrics.description: A functor F from category C to D assigns to each object X in C an object F(X) in D and to each morphism f : X → Y a morphism F(f) with F(1) = 1 and F(f ◦ g) = F(f) ◦ F(g). Covariant functors preserve arrow direction; contravariant functors reverse it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Singular homology H_n is the composition of two functors: singular chain complex functor (spaces → chain complexes) and algebraic homology functor (chain complexes → sequences of abelian groups). Other illustrative examples: dual vector space as contravariant functor, chain complexes as a category, homotopy category of spaces. Functoriality is a required structural property of homology theories.
